# Results

## *Sasa* expanded by a net +19% over 9 years {#sec-res-change}

The area classified as *Sasa* (geodesic area) increased from 8,542 m² in 2012 to 10,170 m² in 2021, a **net change of +1,628 m² (+19%)** over 9 years. This net change reflects the difference between **gross expansion** of 4,095 cells (non-*Sasa*→*Sasa*; 48% of the 2012 area) and **gross loss** of 2,468 cells (*Sasa*→non-*Sasa*; 29%) (@fig-sasa-change; the full transition matrix is in Table S1; the nominal area of a cell is 1 m² and differs from its geodesic area by <0.1%). Expansion originated mainly from other vegetation (53%) and dwarf pine (35%), with the three deciduous shrub classes (rowans, maple, and montane alder) together accounting for 12%. Loss was predominantly to dwarf pine (47%) and other vegetation (38%), with the three deciduous shrub classes together accounting for 15%. Dwarf pine and *Sasa* exchanged area in both directions (interpretation in @sec-disc-change). In the blind interpretation of paired images, 73–87% of loss cells were assigned to boundary ambiguity, a proportion essentially unchanged from that in stable controls (80–85%). Canopy cover was assigned to 22% (8/37) of *Sasa*→dwarf pine transition cells, only slightly above the corresponding judgement for stable dwarf pine controls (15%, 3/20). Thus, the nature of transitions in individual 1 m cells could not be resolved at the photographic scale (Supplementary Information). A few mapped 2021 *Sasa* cells were isolated from all 2012 *Sasa* cells, but these could not be distinguished from classification noise, and no isolated new patches were visually confirmed.

## Snowmelt timing followed microtopographic gradients, with no significant trend detected over 10 years {#sec-res-snow}

Snowmelt climatology ranged from approximately DOY 120 to 230 across the slope, following a ridge-to-hollow gradient (Figure S2). Per-pixel linear trends were negative in 91.7% of cells (mean −0.71 days/year, median −0.63, SD 0.63; Figure S3), but annual spatial means varied markedly among years and showed no significant landscape-scale trend (−0.69 days/year, 95% confidence interval −2.24 to +0.87, p = 0.34; Figure S1). Only 2.0% of cells had individually significant slopes (p < 0.05), and none remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction. Given the power limitations described in @sec-snowmelt, the record for this period is consistent with a gradual advance in snowmelt but does not demonstrate it; trends are used below only to define scenarios.

## Environmentally suitable area greatly exceeded occupied area (Model A) {#sec-res-modelA}

The main Model A, covering the full elevation range, achieved a held-out TSS of 0.78 (mean across 4 spatial blocks; range 0.72–0.85) and an AUC of 0.95. Four members remained in the LASSO blend: 2 gradient boosted tree models, 1 MaxEnt model, and 1 random forest, with boosted trees and MaxEnt accounting for 95% of the blend weight. Response curves (@fig-response-A) showed high habitat suitability at a snowmelt climatology of approximately DOY 150–185, peaking near DOY 172 and declining in later-melting snowbeds. Thus, *Sasa* had a favourable range of snowmelt timing. Habitat suitability also declined with elevation and peaked at intermediate slopes. Responses to TPI, TWI, and aspect components were weaker and non-monotonic. Because estimates of suitable area depend strongly on the binarisation threshold, we primarily used the threshold of 0.16 that maximised TSS on held-out predictions (full threshold sensitivity in Table S2). At this threshold, suitable area was 164×10³ m², approximately 16 times the observed occupied area of 10.2×10³ m². Suitable area consistently exceeded occupied area at thresholds up to 0.55 (@fig-models-AB a).

Grey bands along the bottom of the panels show the distribution (density) of each predictor in presence cells.](files/fig03_response_curves.png){#fig-response-A width=100%}

## Establishment depended strongly on distance from the existing front (Model B) {#sec-res-modelB}

Of the 1,197,536 cells that were non-*Sasa* in 2012, 4,095 had become *Sasa* by 2021. The establishment GAM discriminated well between establishment and non-establishment cells in leave-one-block-out evaluation (pooled AUC 0.946, TSS 0.75; block-specific AUC 0.91–0.96). The gradient boosted tree ensemble fitted to the same folds achieved an AUC of 0.948, indicating that the additive model captured nearly all the signal available to a more flexible learner. Distance from the 2012 front was the strongest term. The 9-year establishment probability declined from approximately 10% within 5 m of the front to approximately 1% at 5–10 m and below 0.1% beyond 80 m. Fitted distance-band probabilities closely matched observed establishment rates throughout the range (@fig-models-AB e; the largest discrepancy was 0.5 percentage points in the 0–5 m band). Environmental associations were consistent with Model A: establishment probability was higher at late-melting (but not the latest-melting) sites, at lower elevations, and on gentler slopes. The map of 9-year establishment probability evaluated from the 2021 front (@fig-models-AB b) was concentrated in narrow bands around existing patches, with the highest values along their lower, late-melting edges.

## Projected establishment continued near existing fronts, with limited sensitivity to snowmelt scenarios {#sec-res-projection}

The cellular automaton initialised from the 2012 distribution reproduced the observed 2012–2021 gross expansion (expected 4,414 m², observed 4,093 m²; ratio 1.08; cell-level AUC 0.92). This was a calibration check. In independent spatial validation, in which each block was predicted by a model never exposed to that block, AUC ranged from 0.79 to 0.86, whereas block-level ratios of expected to observed area ranged from 0.67 to 2.0. Discrimination of establishment *location* was stable across blocks, but prediction errors in the *amount* of establishment were substantial.

Starting from the 2021 distribution, expected new establishment area by 2030 was **4,901 m² under the no-change scenario (s = 0; SD across replicates 70)** and **5,730 m² under continued snowmelt advance at the observed rate (s = −0.71 days/year; SD 84)**, the latter 17% greater than the former (@fig-ca-projection). Both trajectories were nearly linear over 9 years, and both were of similar magnitude to the observed 2012–2021 gross expansion (geodesic area 4,093 m²). Establishment probability was highest along the lower, snowbed-facing edges of existing patches and negligible more than a few tens of metres from any patch (@fig-ca-projection a, b). The extreme scenario at the lower confidence limit of the trend (s = −2.24 days/year) yielded 5,524 m², slightly *less* than the point-estimate scenario (Table S3). Projected area was not a monotonic function of earlier snowmelt (mechanism discussed in @sec-disc-drivers). Structural sensitivity of the projections is reported in the Supplementary Information (Table S9).

## Near-term risk was concentrated in two snowbed communities adjoining existing patches {#sec-res-risk}

Within cells classified as other vegetation in 2021, the expected establishment area by 2030 was 2,429 m² (s = 0) and 3,383 m² (s = −0.71 days/year) (@fig-risk a). Overlain on the Ministry of the Environment's 1:25,000 vegetation map, 73–74% of this expected area fell in the *Fauria crista-galli*–*Carex blepharicarpa* snowbed community and a further 15–16% in the *Anaphalis alpicola*–*Phyllodoce aleutica* snowbed community; together, approximately nine tenths of the expected area lay in snowbed vegetation. The remaining tenth was mapped as dwarf pine community, reflecting the coarse polygons of the Ministry's vegetation map rather than establishment within dwarf pine canopies (@fig-risk b). Observed 2012–2021 establishment had a similar composition (67%, 11%, and 22%, respectively; Table S4). The seed-dispersal stratum, Model A's suitable area within other vegetation in 2021 at the TSS-maximising threshold, was more than an order of magnitude larger (Figure S5).
